steps.prompt: What does the to + verb mean here?
options: It gives the reason — why the person did it.
It is part of the main verb of the sentence.
It shows that the action is in the future.
steps.answer: It gives the reason — why the person did it.
steps.why: This is the infinitive of purpose. It answers Why?

steps.title: Uses of the infinitive with to
steps.html:
PatternExample
to give a reasonI spoke to an architect to find out more.
after my job / my role isMy job is to advise clients.
after certain verbsThey decided to move the desks.
after it’s + adjectiveIt’s important to show what you have finished.
in order to (formal)They moved the desks in order to encourage communication.
for + nounI went there for a meeting.
for + -ing (what a thing is for)This room is for having informal meetings.

The commonest way to say why is simply to + base form: I called to ask about the job.

Never use for + base form: say I came here to study, not for study.

Use for + a noun: I came here for a meeting. Use for + -ing when you describe what a thing is used for: a room for having meetings.

In order to means the same as to but sounds formal. In speech, plain to is normal.

After it’s + an adjective, use to + base form: It’s important to ask. It’s difficult to train somebody remotely.

You met You use it to … in Lesson 15, when you explained a word. This is the same structure.

steps.title: The changing face of work
steps.html:
Three changes, and one that is harder to see.

Reading

Ten years ago, almost nobody in this city worked from home. Today about one office worker in three does it at least two days a week. The job titles have not changed. Almost everything else has.

The first change is where the work happens. A remote job is done entirely away from the office; a hybrid job is split between the two. Companies did not choose this to be kind. They did it to keep the people they had already trained, and to save the rent on half a floor.

The second change is what a job actually involves. Ask somebody what they do and they will name a profession. Ask what their week involves and you get something else: “It is my job to advise clients, but most of the week is spent in meetings.” “One of my main roles is to recruit new staff.” “I’m in charge of the day-to-day business, so I do a lot of paperwork.” The title is the smallest part of the answer.

The third change is harder to see. When the office was the only place to work, being present looked like working. Now it is important to show what you have finished, not how long you sat there. That is easier for people who write things down and harder for people who do not.

None of this is only good news. It is difficult to train somebody remotely, and it is easy to disappear in a company you never visit. But the direction is clear: the question at an interview is no longer “where will you sit?” It is “what are you here to do?”

steps.answer: Sets dates for cases, answers enquiries and deals with emails.
steps.html:
Three changes, and one that is harder to see.

Reading

Ten years ago, almost nobody in this city worked from home. Today about one office worker in three does it at least two days a week. The job titles have not changed. Almost everything else has.

The first change is where the work happens. A remote job is done entirely away from the office; a hybrid job is split between the two. Companies did not choose this to be kind. They did it to keep the people they had already trained, and to save the rent on half a floor.

The second change is what a job actually involves. Ask somebody what they do and they will name a profession. Ask what their week involves and you get something else: “It is my job to advise clients, but most of the week is spent in meetings.” “One of my main roles is to recruit new staff.” “I’m in charge of the day-to-day business, so I do a lot of paperwork.” The title is the smallest part of the answer.

The third change is harder to see. When the office was the only place to work, being present looked like working. Now it is important to show what you have finished, not how long you sat there. That is easier for people who write things down and harder for people who do not.

None of this is only good news. It is difficult to train somebody remotely, and it is easy to disappear in a company you never visit. But the direction is clear: the question at an interview is no longer “where will you sit?” It is “what are you here to do?”
